subject: math
title: Word Problems to 50
seo_title: Grade 1 Math Word Problems to 50 Worksheets: Join, Take Away and Compare (Ontario)
standard_text: Use objects, diagrams, and equations to represent, describe, and solve situations involving addition and subtraction of whole numbers that add up to no more than 50
meta_desc: Free Grade 1 math worksheets on word problems to 50, matched to the Ontario curriculum: join and take-away stories with pictures, compare stories, bar models and choosing the equation. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Picture the story. Then decide: add or subtract?
key_sub: Some more come: add. Some go away: subtract. “How many more” means find the difference, so subtract. Draw it, then write an equation with a ☐ for the missing number.
body_html:
The idea: picture the story

Read the story. Ask: what happens? Do some come? Do some go away? Are two groups compared? Then find the number you do not know.

StoryWhat happensEquation
JoinSome more come.5 + 3 = ☐
Take awaySome go away.9 − 4 = ☐
CompareWhich has more? How many more?8 − 5 = ☐
Part-part-wholeTwo parts make the whole.24 + 5 = ☐

Join: some more come

Draw the first group. Draw the ones that come. Count them all.

Take away: some go away

Draw them all. Cross out the ones that go away. Count the ones that are left.

With bigger numbers, use tens and ones. Take away tens from the tens.

Compare: how many more?

Line up the two rows. Match them one to one. The extra ones are the answer.

Part-part-whole: use a bar model

The long bar is the whole. The two short bars are the parts. Know both parts? Add. Know the whole and one part? Subtract.

Choose the equation

Ava had 15 stickers. Her teacher gave her some more. Now she has 35. How many did she get?

The number added is missing. Put the ☐ there: 15 + ☐ = 35. 15 + 20 = 35, so the ☐ is 20.

Answer: 15 + ☐ = 35, 20 stickers

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Adding in a take-away story: 9 − 4 is not 13Some go away, so there are fewer. Subtract: 9 − 4 = 5.
Adding in a “how many more” storyLine up the rows. Count the extra ones: 8 − 5 = 3.
Using the wrong numbers: giving 9 or 4 as the answerFind the number you do not know. Check it in the story.
Adding tens as ones: 23 + 20 = 2520 is 2 tens. 2 tens + 2 tens = 4 tens. 23 + 20 = 43.

faq.q: What word problems do Grade 1 students solve in the Ontario math curriculum?
faq.a: Grade 1 students solve join, take-away, compare and part-part-whole stories with whole numbers that add up to no more than 50. They use objects, drawings and equations to show and solve each story.

faq.q: How can I help my child with “how many more” questions?
faq.a: Line up two rows of objects and match them one to one. The extra objects are the answer, so 8 apples and 5 apples gives 8 − 5 = 3 more.

faq.q: What is a bar model in Grade 1 math?
faq.a: A bar model shows a whole as a long bar and its two parts as shorter bars under it. If both parts are known, add; if the whole and one part are known, subtract.

faq.q: Should Grade 1 students use key words to solve word problems?
faq.a: Not by themselves. Words like “more” can trick children, so have them act out or draw the story first and then decide to add or subtract.

items.e: You know both parts. Find the whole, so add. Put them together: 8 + 5 = 13. Answer: 13 books.

sets.title: Choose the equation for the story

items.q: At recess, 10 children were on the playground. Then 5 more children came out. How many children are on the playground now? Which equation matches the story?
items.e: Some are added and the end is missing, so add: 10 + 5 = ☐. The ☐ is 15. (10 − 5 = ☐ does not match the story.)

items.q: The class library had 12 books. The teacher added some more. Now there are 19 books in the class library. How many books did the teacher add? Which equation matches the story?
items.e: The number added is missing, so the ☐ goes in the middle: 12 + ☐ = 19. The ☐ is 7. (12 + 19 = ☐ does not match the story.)
